study.title: Judges 15 - Samson, Conflicts with the Philistines and the Suspension of God
study.overview: Judges 15 shows Samson in a sequence of clashes that are born of personal offenses, but end up reaching the Philistine oppression over Israel. The chapter alternates human initiative, escalation violence and clear interventions of the Spirit of the Lord. Samson acts with a strong sense of revenge, but the narrator points out that God uses it to hurt the Philistines, support his servant in weakness, and continue to judge them in favor of Israel.

outline.title: Samson returns, is rejected and responds with judgment on the harvests
outline.explanation: Samson goes to his wife with a gift as a sign of reconciliation, but finds that she has been given to another man. The refusal of the father-in-law provokes in him a response against the Philistines: he destroys plantations, vineyards and olive groves with foxes and torches, reaching the economy of the enemy.

outline.title: The cruelty of the Philistines and the Revenge of Samson
outline.explanation: The Philistines burn Samson's wife and her father. Samson responds with a great death, and then shelters in a cave, showing that the conflict has passed from the domestic sphere to an open war.

outline.title: Judah gives Samson, but God strengthens him to overcome a thousand men
outline.explanation: The Philistines press Judah to capture Samson. The men of Judah tie him up and deliver him, but the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him: the cords undo, he kills a thousand men with the complaint of an asn and gives name to the place of victory.

outline.title: The thirst of Samson and the faithfulness of God in sustaining him
outline.explanation: After the victory, Samson cries out to God by water, acknowledging that salvation came from the Lord and asking that he does not die from thirst. God opens a cavity and makes water come out, and the chapter concludes by summarizing that Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the Philistine period.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the continued pressure of the Philistines on Israel, mentioned in the narrative itself and in the notes. Judah appears as a people who live with this domination and fears an open conflict. The notes also indicate that Samson's twenty years of judgment occurred at the time of Israel's bondage to the Philistines. There is no basis in the notes provided, the basis for broadening the context with geographical or historical details in addition.
study.theology: The text presents a tension between human action and divine sovereignty. Samson acts moved by anger and desire for retribution, but the narrator and commentators insist that the Spirit of the LORD empowers him and directs him in decisive moments. Thus, the chapter does not celebrate violence as a moral ideal; it shows God using an imperfect deliverer to confront Philistine oppression. Samson's thirst is also theologically important: after a great victory, he remains dependent on God. The water received miraculously teaches that the same God who grants triumph also sustains the life of his servant. The closure with the twenty-year judgment reinforces that Samson is not only an isolated warrior, but an instrument of God's rule over Israel in a period of foreign domination.

scholarViews.insight: Samson bears gifts to his wife as a gesture of reconciliation; Henry understands this act as generous, coming from whom he had been offended, and notes that the goal was to restore peace.
Clarke notes that the Philistines did not want to break with Israel in general; they especially wanted to arrest Samson, because it was the cause of their damage.

questions: What does the chapter teach about the difference between personal vengeance and God's purpose in acting through an imperfect deliverer?
How does the reaction of the men of Judah reveal the effect of prolonged oppression on the courage of God's people?
How does Samson's thirst, just after victory, correct any spiritual pride or excessive confidence in himself?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader not to confuse success with self-reliance. When God grants victory, we still need to recognize our thirst, our limitation and our dependence on it. It also invites us to examine how we react to offenses: Samson often responds with anger and retribution, but the text shows that God can act despite this, not because human revenge is a model to be imitated. In practice, it is better to seek justice with humility, to refuse passivity to evil and, at the same time, to depend on the Lord for sustenance, direction and self-control.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided clearly support Samson's reading as an instrument of God, the human humiliation of his thirst, and the Philistine intention to capture Samson without total war against Israel. However, there is no basis for notes to affirm additional details about the emotional motivation of all the characters, nor to reconstruct with broader historical accuracy than the chapter itself states. There is also Clarke's observation about the meaning of a word in 15:15, but it is speculative; therefore, the study did not deal it as a decisive interpretation.
